Labour for Palestine – Canada celebrates the Canadian Labour Congress — Canadian Council’s endorsement of General Resolution ‘061’.

October 28th, 2026 the Canadian Council of the CLC passed a resolution declaring trade, services and relationship with Israel “hot cargo”, endorsed the Arms Embargo Now campaign and vowed to work with unions to make weapons and military equipment destined to Israel “hot cargo,” not to be touched by workers of conscience in line with the resolution and hot cargo declaration. title: European dockers to strike against war (Socialist Worker-UK)
content:
Workers are ‘calling for an end to war, austerity and to threats to trade union freedoms’

Dockers strike comes as revolts spread across Europe (Photo: sicobas.lavoratoriautorganizzati.9/Facebook)

Ports across the Mediterranean will shut down this Friday as workers at over 100 in 17 countries go on strike.

For years, military cargo used to ravage Palestine has gone through civilian ports across the world.

These workers are uniting their demands over pay and conditions with the fightback against war and genocide.

Giorgos Gogos, president of the Dockworkers’ Union of Piraeus Port Authority in Greece, spoke to Socialist Worker about the action.

He said, “We have called a global day of action against the militarisation of ports and war. We are calling for an end to austerity and to threats to trade unions’ freedoms.

“Across the world, armed conflicts are increasing instability and insecurity,” he said. “People are bleeding for the profits of imperialists and capitalists.

“Plans for militarisation like the European Union’s ReArm Europe project affect all European ports, states, societies and citizens,” he said.

“There is international dialogue between dockers in the European Dockworkers Council and many others.

“Dockworkers have a tradition of international cooperation. We have struggled and won together many times.”

The strike comes as revolts are spreading across Europe.

author: labor4pal
title: ICE Is Running One of the Largest Anti-Left Surveillance Operations in US History (Wired)
content:
ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations is engaged in far-reaching spying against left-wing activists that rivals the FBI and CIA crackdowns on the Civil Rights and anti-war movements.

Attorneys for 15 Minnesota residents facing federal conspiracy charges have obtained evidence of a sweeping, possibly unconstitutional spying operation carried out by Immigration and Customs Enforcement against left-wing social movements in Minnesota and beyond.

The high-profile Minnesota 15 prosecution makes clear that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), flush with federal funds and newly hired personnel, is now President Donald Trump’s primary tool against dissent, with a powerful array of post-9/11 investigative authorities brought to bear against everyday Americans organizing their communities.

Nothing of this scale has been seen in the United States, experts say, since the federal government’s counterinsurgency against the New Left and the anti-war movement in the 1960s and 1970s.

Among the records revealed during the discovery process in these cases are dozens of reports, audio transcripts, emails, intercepted Signal chats, photographs, database queries, and more. They reveal the inner workings of the domestic terrorism investigations, running under the names Project Whipple Shield and Operation Puppet Master, authorized by the controversial National Security Presidential Memorandum 7.

Published following Charlie Kirk’s assassination in September of last year, NSPM 7 instructs federal law enforcement to use every tool available against organizations and people who criticize the administration’s policies and espouse “anti-Christian” ideas. The full scope and extent of the investigations it authorizes remains unknown.

Defense attorneys for the Minnesota 15 claim that the prosecution stems from a broader nationwide surveillance operation aimed at opponents of the Trump administration’s immigration policies. One attorney in the case directly compares the DHS-run campaign to the FBI’s infamous Counterintelligence Program, or COINTELPRO, which unconstitutionally surveilled, infiltrated, and blackmailed racial justice, civil rights, and anti-war movements from the 1950s through the early 1970s.

Three former law enforcement officials who reviewed filings concur, telling WIRED that the case is almost certainly part of a wider intelligence-gathering operation that began long before the administration invaded Minnesota in December 2025.

Dueling motions in the case over discovery of DHS’s surveillance program reveal that personnel with Homeland Security Investigations—one of ICE’s two components—repurposed funding mechanisms and investigative tools for serious criminal probes and turned them on domestic dissenters. Operation Keyhole, the HSI undercover program that bankrolled the Minnesota 15 prosecution, dates back to 2008. As of June 2026, it was underwriting a half dozen active undercover investigations in the Minneapolis–Saint Paul area.

Around 120 HSI agents, many drawn from specialized units across the country that have served as the leading edge of the administration’s militarized immigration enforcement operations, were assigned to the case—including 11 undercovers. They used highly invasive surveillance techniques, including the deployment of Reaper drones and Patriot Act tools usually restricted to money laundering and terrorism investigations. Undercover operatives also infiltrated churches in apparent violation of a court order.

The Minnesota 15 indictment stems from the Trump administration’s demand that the Justice Department “go big and go loud” to crack down on community response networks during last winter’s Operation Metro Surge. Twin Cities activists organized volunteers to monitor DHS agents and their vehicles using encrypted Signal groups, homebuilt vehicle databases, and a centralized dispatch system. Government prosecutors claim that this amounts to a criminal conspiracy to block immigration enforcement, unlawfully identify and stalk federal agents, and even assault them.

Their defense attorneys say the heavy charges filed against the Minnesota 15 don’t align with their alleged conduct. “This is the first time I’ve had a client who’s accused of a conspiracy and went on a speaking tour,” says Kevin Riach, who represents defendant Isaac Sant.

An internal ICE document laying out the scope of Operation Puppet Master—which led to the indictment of the Minneapolis 15—ends by noting, “This case has also been accepted under CUC Op Keyhole.” According to prosecutors, Operation Keyhole is a long-standing program created by HSI’s Saint Paul office to fund “undercover activity”—primarily equipment purchases and personnel costs—in a region covering Minnesota, North and South Dakota, Iowa, and Nebraska. The program has funded at least 77 investigations into “narcotics trafficking, child sexual abuse, financial investigations, and counter-proliferation” since it started in December 2008.

The CUC prefix, per an internal 2008 DHS handbook unearthed by the independent media outlet Unicorn Riot, refers to Certified Undercover Operations, a formal designation with clearly defined oversight mechanisms, procedures, and reporting requirements. Operation Keyhole’s parameters are reviewed every six months by a committee comprising senior DOJ and DHS officials. As of June 2026, when it was last renewed, Keyhole funded six active investigations, including Project Whipple Shield, which was initiated in February to probe claims of assault, stalking, and doxing of DHS agents and other federal employees, and underpins the Minnesota 15 indictment.

At least 11 undercover agents working under Operation Keyhole infiltrated Twin Cities anti-ICE activists, participating in martial arts and know-your-rights trainings, marches, general strikes, and community meetings. They also infiltrated activists’ communications network for identifying possible undercover ICE vehicles and dispatching activists to tail them through the Twin Cities, and penetrated several activist group chats on Signal, transmitting their contents back to other HSI colleagues for analysis and eventual inclusion in the indictment.

Activist conferences as far away as Seattle, Michigan, Chicago, and New York City were placed under surveillance as part of the investigation, and HSI teams photographed and ran the license plates of every car parked in the lot of a meeting location or seen transporting activists. There is also drone footage from unarmed Customs and Border Protection Reaper drones of the activists moving around the Twin Cities area.

The undercovers were part of a much broader group of more than 50 HSI agents, including at least two dozen from HSI’s little-known Special Operations Group, that took part in the investigation and surveillance of the defendants, both digital and in-person. Feds with decades of experience on complex financial crimes, drug cartel investigations, human trafficking, and organized crime were pulled into the Minnesota 15 investigation.

Several of the Minnesota 15 case agents are from out of state and appear in court records for the prosecutions of anti-ICE activists in other cities. This includes Los Angeles–based HSI agents Robert Kurtz III, who specializes in financial fraud, and Ryan Ribner, who allegedly assaulted SEIU California president David Huerta at a June 2025 protest of an ICE enforcement operation, arrested him, and then claimed the then 58-year-old Huerta attacked federal law enforcement. (Huerta’s charges were dropped in July after videos contradicting Ribner’s account surfaced.) HSI records show Ribner was also involved in at least two prosecutions of Southern California residents who physically confronted ICE and Border Patrol agents last year.

Other agents from the conspiracy investigation have also been involved in recent high-profile incidents. Tim Gerber, the “team leader” of an HSI Special Operations Group squad, led the investigation of former CNN host Don Lemon for reporting on a protest at a Minneapolis Church where an ICE agent was a pastor. Fellow SOG agent Yue Her was present at the scene of a 2025 incident when Renee Good’s killer, ICE Special Response Team agent Johnathan Ross, was dragged by the car of a man he tried to apprehend.

“This operation does not seem in any way limited to Minnesota,” says Spencer Reynolds, a former DHS attorney and counterterrorism lawyer who now works at the NAACP Legal Defense Fund. “As we saw with the boots on the ground in the streets, with Greg Bovino leading CBP and Border Patrol special forces units on sweeping raids across the country, this is the intelligence and undercover investigative apparatus that is running in parallel to the door-kicking.”

Mike German, a retired FBI agent who worked undercover domestic terrorism cases for years before becoming a sharp critic of post-9/11 federal law enforcement, likens the Minnesota 15 case to federal law enforcement’s long history of suppressing left-wing social movements, including the CIA’s Operation MH/Chaos, which surveilled the anti-war movement during the Vietnam War for evidence of foreign influence. One difference is the sheer scale—this time, it’s bigger.

According to a 2011 book by former CIA officer Frank Rafalko, the CIA secret investigation into suspected foreign influence on the New Left and anti-Vietnam War movement had 42 officers working the case at its peak. Court records show 119 HSI agents worked on the Minnesota 15 case alone.

“Broad monitoring of social media, communications, and financial transactions are used to link an ever increasing number of people as potential subjects of investigation and prosecution,” German says. “These are exactly the kind of intelligence activities J. Edgar Hoover adopted to suppress the Civil Rights and anti-war movements in the 1960s.”

The key difference today, German says, is the vast pool of data available to the feds.

HSI used highly invasive measures—including scrutiny of wire transfers, PayPal reimbursements, and other financial transactions; forensic digital analysis of website traffic; 15 terabytes worth of infiltrated Signal chats; and information from a commercial data broker—to identify individuals under investigation.

After a local activist uploaded a license-plate search tool on Fly.io, a developer-focused public cloud platform, to an infiltrated Signal chat, HSI agents reviewed website DNS queries and Stripe data along with data purchased from a commercial broker. This gave HSI access to SSH session logs, outbound connection records, the Fly.io account’s signup IP, and a Stripe card fingerprint on an account that had never completed a payment. Agents fused that with Minnesota DVS records and commercial data from the Thomson-Reuters CLEAR platform to produce a driver’s license number, Social Security number summary, years of address history, phone numbers, property records, and jointly registered vehicles.

Documents concerning financial records requested through the Treasury Department’s 314(a) suspicious activity reporting program—created by the Patriot Act to enable speedy tracking of finances for terrorism and money-laundering investigations—show that the feds targeted records of 29 “subjects” during queries conducted on March 31, 2026. Emails viewed by WIRED between several HSI agents based in Los Angeles and Arizona show that batches of records were turned over pursuant to those inquiries, including some dealing with SEIU that a senior Minnesota HSI agent sent to a LA-based colleague to be filed “wherever these records are stored.”

HSI investigators used similar workarounds to warrants and grand jury subpoenas to obtain phone records for several journalists who covered Operation Metro Surge, as first reported by The Guardian. Court records show the feds used an administrative summons request reserved for violations of customs and taxation requirements, which does not fit the activity that made up the criminal charges filed by the Minnesota US attorney against former CNN anchor Don Lemon and others.

The Minnesota 15 case is the clearest example yet of DHS pursuing the Trump administration’s efforts to crack down on what have long been upheld as First Amendment–protected activities. But it’s unlikely alone.

Riach, the defense attorney, says the HSI reports show the agency is complicit in what he called “the new COINTELPRO.”

“What we saw during the immigration surges last year was that ICE is the administration’s paramilitary force, the projector of strength,” Riach says. “Here, we see that HSI are taking the FBI’s place as the investigative secret police—it’s the classic one-two punch of authoritarian regimes around the world.”

author: labor4pal
title: Motown and the Making of Working-Class Revolutionaries: an Interview with Jerome Scott and Walda Katz-Fishman (UAWD Daily Struggle)
content:
Anthony Stoner October 26, 2026

Jerome Scott and Walda Katz-Fishman, authors of Motown and the Making of Working-Class Revolutionaries: The League of Revolutionary Black Workers, share their reflections on the UAW’s Black radical tradition, the tactic of the wildcat strike, and the importance of unions fighting for the working class as a whole.

In the 1960s, Chrysler—the only Big Three corporation whose operations remained largely in Detroit at the time—began to hire Black workers, many fresh from the U.S. South. They had the worst and most dangerous jobs, and Chrysler frequently fired them before they obtained UAW contract protections after a 90-day probation. In 1968, these conditions and the lack of representation by the white-dominated UAW—at that time led by Walter Reuther, whose “Administration Caucus” dominated the union then and for decades after his death led to a wildcat strike in the Dodge Main plant initiated by the Dodge Revolutionary Union Movement (DRUM) (A wildcat strike is a strike not officially authorized by a union). A number of other RUMs were then created around Detroit, and in 1969 the League of Revolutionary Black Workers (LRBW) was founded by Black militant labor organizers to help unite and aid struggles around the city. Among those organizers was Jerome Scott, who, along with Walda Katz-Fishman, has written an account of the LRBW, based on extensive interviews with surviving members of the League, their families and comrades. Their book, Motown and the Making of Working-Class Revolutionaries: The Story of the League of Revolutionary Black Workers, is available from University of Georgia Press.

—Anthony Stoner, UAW Local 4811

Anthony SToner: Why were wildcat strikes the tactic both DRUM and then the LRBW focused on? What’s the role of a wildcat strike for today?

Jerome scott: The wildcat strike became our principal tactic mainly because it was a two-edged sword. We could attack the company as well as struggle with the union. The company of course was and is the major enemy, but back in the day, and in some unions even today, the collaboration between the union and the corporation is not good for the workers themselves. And so we realized after the first wildcat strike (for us, and the first in the country for about fifty years) at Dodge Main that that wildcat strike really did attack both of our struggles. What we didn’t realize when we started it was that it was also a very offensive tactic. We were making the decisions; and the corporation and the union had to respond and defend against that, rather than the workers always being on the defensive. So the wildcat strike was a hell of a weapon.

AS: How did Doug Fraser [then head of UAW Chrysler Department] and the UAW International use the “flying squadron” during the 1973 wildcat?

JS: A little bit on the history of the flying squadron. It started with the United Mine Workers movement in Appalachia because of the rolling strikes that happened in the organizing of that union. It was an organized group of union members that they would take from strike event to strike event and try to make sure that nobody crossed the picket line. They were an apparatus that actually really backed up the picket lines in the strikes that were held in the heyday of organizing the UAW, the United Mine Workers, and so on. And the purpose was really to let the workers know that the International was part of this strike. So the concept of the flying squadron had a long tradition of respect from the union movement.

In our case, in our strike at Chrysler in 1973, we were able to shut down the entire Chrysler corporation for about a week; and that was because of the strategic nature of the Detroit Forge plant where I worked. There was only one other plant in the world that made the same parts that we made and it was a forging plant in [apartheid-era] South Africa. The corporation had done all it could do to try to break our strike, and try to break the picket line, but the picket line was going on 24/7.

What we learned later is that the corporation had called Solidarity House and said, “you have to do something about this strike.” And it was then that Fraser organized the historic flying squadron to come break our picket line rather than support it. And it was a pitched battle—it wasn’t like we saw them coming and laid down our picket signs—it was a big struggle. But eventually they were able to break our picket line and end our struggle after a week. Now the company decided that they would permanently fire three of us. But later on we learned that the company didn’t decide who to fire—the company left it up to the union to decide. They fired two Black workers and one white worker, two production workers and one skilled trades worker. The two Black workers were in the League of Revolutionary Black Workers leading up to that strike, and the skilled trades person was someone we had worked with in our plant over the previous two years. So not only did they bring out the flying squadron to break our strike, they also collaborated with the company to decide who would be permanently fired.

Now, that permanent fire for the three of us sort of backfired on them, because one of the skilled tradesmen who was out on the wildcat strike was also in the process of buying a bar across the street from the plant we had just shut down, and across the street from six other Chrysler plants up and down that block. So he hired the three of us as bartenders, and that became the best job we had ever had. Because once you shut down the corporation and people knew you were in this fight with the union and the company, they wanted to talk to us. So we had a constant flow of workers coming into the bar, having political discussions, trying to figure out how they could have a wildcat strike at their shop.

AS: Why do you think the International was acting this way—was it mostly racism, was it also their investments in the company?

JS: The 70s was a period when the unions were really trying to collaborate with corporations to have these “Joint Work Committees” on the shop floor with the foremen and the workers. They were promoting this whole idea that we could have peace in the working-class battle between the owners of the Chrysler corporation and the workers. So it was this notion, I think, that we could have this “peaceful” period, where they wouldn’t have to strike, they wouldn’t have to do the real fight for workers, but the corporation would somehow allow them to make advances.

I think there’s one other thing that played into this: early on in the 50s, unions made a decision that they would only represent their members, and not the working class as a whole, and so they saw this peaceful coexistence with the corporation as a way to support their members and separate themselves from the struggles of the working class as a whole and concentrate on just the relations between their members and the corporations as opposed to the struggles between the working class and the corporations.

WALDA katz-fishman: The workers also did some investigation, and they found out the union was actually invested in the corporation and was making more money from its investments than from the actual dues from its members. So it was not just a political collaboration, it was really an economic merging of the interests of the “union hierarchy” and the corporation. And that’s pretty extraordinary: Y’all should do some investigation today.

AS: Your book discusses the idea of union organizing for the working class as a whole rather than just representing the members of the union. Why is that important? What can we do with that today?

When you struggle for higher wages in a shop, that really does affect the whole community around it. And so if you fight and bring in the communities around the shops and bring in whatever motion around police brutality or the fight against poverty or any of those community-based fights, they’re all working-class fights.

JS: It’s more important today than it’s ever been. When the trade union movement was developing in this country, it developed on the basis of representing the working class. Back in the 30s and 40s, there were at least 9 or 10 international unions that demanded the end of capitalism as the way for workers to actually get and hold what they were fighting for. So the trade union movement has a revolutionary guts to it that they’ve been trying to stomp out ever since. I think it was during the McCarthy era in the early 50s, one of the demands that the ruling class made on the union movement—well of course, one of them was to rid itself of any communists that existed in the leadership and try to scorch its membership as well. But one of the other demands was that they had to stop trying to mobilize the working class as part of the union struggle and only concentrate on their members. And the corporations would then back off on the struggle around contracts and give them easier access to making contracts. So the leadership of the international trade union movement made that agreement. They agreed that they would concentrate on their membership.

The reason it’s so important is because when you struggle for higher wages in a shop, that really does affect the whole community around it. And so if you fight and bring in the communities around the shops and bring in whatever motion around police brutality or the fight against poverty or any of those community-based fights, they’re all working-class fights. And a trade union struggle in the middle of that can add a lot of power and prestige to those struggles as well as provide the trade union with support from the community that will also have an effect on their battle in the shop.

We have got to understand that we’re in a much more powerful position if we approach it from the standpoint of a broad-based front of struggle to organize a shop. Not just the workers in it, but their families, the community that it sits in, the drivers that service it, the whole shebang. And more or less a working-class strategy for organizing a union rather than a membership-based strategy for organizing a union.

WKF: Huge sections of the working class, the academy, professors and scientists and doctors and nurses and the whole tech industry that has not been historically unionized, are losing jobs. They’re losing jobs, job security, certainly benefits, and so we’re in a class war. And so to develop that class consciousness when the trade union movement is such a small percentage of the working class, it’s really important for us to think about the working class as a whole, and it’s really important for that section that is more highly organized to help broaden out the understanding of who we are, what our interests are in society, and how do we help lift up and help organize the working class as a whole. And I think some of the unions have played an important role—in May Day Strong, or in the call for a 2028 general strike—so we can see that they have a capacity to take some important “leadership roles,” because they do have resources and organization.

AS: How important was organizing around health and safety issues to expanding League contacts with the non-Black workers in the factory, the white workers, the skilled trade workers, and so on?

JS: Health and safety was a lot bigger than anybody thought, when you think back on it. There were two major things that were really the impetus for wildcat strikes. One of course was the way management treated workers. The whole question of white supremacy in the plants back in the 60s was just as bad as anyplace else. The foremen thought they could treat Black workers any way they wanted to, and treated us like, I’ll fire your ass in a second, if you don’t do as I tell you to do and not argue with me, not discuss with me whether or not it’s legal for me to treat you this way. The other reason was health and safety. Somebody was always getting hurt in the plant, every day. Once we began to reach out to white workers to try to figure out how to build those kinds of relationships, we realized the connecting factor was health and safety, and skilled trades workers were just as concerned that they might get injured on the job as we were as production workers.

WKF: As I recall, it was a white worker whose hand was cut off; that was the provocation for the ‘73 wildcat strike.

WKF: And what the white workers said to you all, the Black workers, we’re really glad you all have been carrying forward this fight. So once they were able to work together, it was better, the wildcat was more powerful when it was a multiracial wildcat.

There has always been multiracial struggle—there’s been Black working-class struggle but also multiracial struggle—in the South against the conditions of life there.

JS: The difference between the wildcats that happened prior to our ‘73 wildcat, which was mainly Black workers that went out and were able to shut down the process of that particular factory for a while. Our ability to shut Chrysler down for a whole week was the difference between having the vast majority of the workers in that shop support the strike versus only Black workers. So it meant all the difference in the world.

AS: Many of the League workers either themselves or their families had come from the South. Why is the South this important battleground in the class war?

WKF: What I think the League expresses is that there has always been multiracial struggle—there’s been Black working-class struggle but also multiracial struggle—in the South against the conditions of life there. There is union organizing in the South, despite Taft-Hartley, which said states can implement state-by-state right-to-work laws, which makes it almost impossible for unions to organize, so the South became the “solid South” of right-to-work. So both in terms of both working-class organizing and in terms of federal policy—economy, ecology, politics, and society, public institutions—the South is either a place where the working class breaks through or the capitalist class manages to control it and therefore the nation. And that’s why the South is such a battleground today, it’s emerging because the working class is in motion, and they know this is the place where it’s easiest for them to grab control back.

JS: The ruling class is once again relying on the fact that if they’re going to consolidate fascism in this country, they have to consolidate it in the South. And therefore they have to get rid of the Voting Rights Act, and they have to prevent unions from spreading across the South in this period where unions are really beginning to pick up again and beginning to organize.

AS: Tell me about the history of the League and its contacts with the PLO (Palestine Liberation Organization) and the Arab Workers Caucus (in the UAW in Dearborn, Michigan), especially given Israel’s genocide and the UAW’s divestment from Israel bonds.

JS: Over the last couple years, we’ve given a lot of thought to this too. We looked at ourselves as oppressed and exploited people—and Detroit and Dearborn was a special sort of area of the country. We had a bigger Middle Eastern population in Dearborn than any other place outside of the Middle East. And that was true because of the recruitment of international workers by the auto industry. They figured that cultural division might slow down the union process. But the fact was that we were working side by side with Middle Eastern folk who had migrated here to the United States and were part of our working-class brothers and sisters. When we learned that the UAW was buying Israeli bonds and that that was supporting the oppression of the Palestinian people, we reached out to our coworkers, and we even had delegations go to the Middle East and meet primarily with the PLO.

We realized it was our country, our government, that was sending all this money to Israel and soliciting our trade unions to use our pension funds, our money, to buy Israeli bonds. So not only did we develop good relations with them, but one of the wildcat strikes back in the day was a wildcat strike against the UAW continuing to buy those bonds. We didn’t appreciate our dues being used to support the oppression and exploitation of another set of oppressed and exploited people. That was the basis of our relationship, and we continued to have those kinds of relationships not only with the Palestinian people—we did the same thing with the Vietnamese people, and the Irish struggle against the British, the whole shebang of oppressed and exploited people—we tried to reach out to and let them know we were all fighting the same kind of fight, only on different fronts.

You have to return to the roots of the trade union movement and make your struggle […] a working-class issue, and any advancements, you want to be applied not only to the workers in that industry but also to the communities in which those workers live and to the section of society which those workers represent.

WKF: So internationalism was a big part of their working-class understanding of the world. It was Edna in our interviews who said what Jerome just said: We organized together because we lived side by side, in the same neighborhoods and worked together. So it was a very concrete unity, as well as an intellectual kind of unity, a political unity.

AS: What does the experience of the League contribute now to militant unionism?

JS: This is a war on the working class—it’s a war on the unions, so you’ve got to act like it’s a war—but it’s also a war on the working class as a whole. You have to return to the roots of the trade union movement and make your struggle, your contracts or whatever issue you’re fighting around, a working-class issue, and any advancements, you want to be applied not only to the workers in that industry but also to the communities in which those workers live and to the section of society which those workers represent. And so there has to be a working-class victory. And in order for there to be a working-class victory, you’ve got to mobilize and educate the working class as a whole.

That would be my message to the UAW. If they want this general strike in 2028 to actually happen and be a success, the mobilization for it has got to be a society, working-class-wide mobilization. When ‘28 comes, you might have those contracts that expire at the same time. But if you don’t have some secondary boycotts organized, if you don’t have some secondary supports mobilized around the logistics industry, then it will not be successful. So it has to be a community-wide effort if we’re going to make this general strike be an advancement for the working class in taking the offensive in this war.

WKF: The only other thing is that if it’s only about 10% of workers—and that’s workers who have jobs—who are unionized, then we’ve got to go back to our working-class roots. The trade union movement has an opportunity to really play a leadership role. But they’ve got to reach deep down to where the working class is, which is outside of the trade union movement, and figure out how to really play that role to build an organized hub of organizing.

title: SUNY BDS* Labor Alliance Call to UUP, GSEU, and RAU Leadership and Members
content:
A post shared by SUNY BDS (@sunybds)

SUNY BDS Labor Alliance Call to UUP, GSEU and RAU Leadership and Members

SUNY BDS* Labor Alliance, composed of United University Professions (UUP), Research Assistants Union (RAU), and Graduate Student Employees Union (GSEU) members, calls on our labor unions to show support for Palestinian liberation, take a stance against the US government’s facilitation of war and genocide in Palestine and the broader Middle East, and stand in solidarity with the international working class by adopting a clear anti-imperialist position.

Israel’s ongoing attacks against the Palestinians result in devastating loss and misery. According to official numbers, Israel has killed 46,707 Palestinians and injured over 110,265 as of January 15, 2025. However, according to numerous scientific studies and on-the-ground health professionals, the estimates of death tolls may be as high as 186,000, representing 7.9% of Gaza’s population. Additionally, 1.9 million people, virtually all of Gaza’s inhabitants, have been displaced, while 66% of all buildings have been damaged, 78% of which are completely destroyed, or severely or moderately damaged.

On January 31, 2024, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Israel’s military engagement in Gaza constitutes a plausible genocide and insisted that the Israeli military immediately cease activities contributing to the destruction of Palestinian life and culture in Gaza. It has been established by multiple genocide scholars, historians and other experts that Israel’s activities in Gaza fit the definition of a genocide. Furthermore, Israel’s actions are made possible by the US. The US has provided Israel with more than $20 billion in military aid since October 7, 2023. ProPublica has revealed that the US government has continued sending aid to Israel, despite internal reporting by the US Agency for International Development (USAID) that Israeli interferes with “aid efforts, including killing aid workers, razing agricultural structures, bombing ambulances and hospitals, sitting on supply depots and routinely turning away trucks full of food and medicine.” US law itself makes it illegal to send weapons to countries that interfere with US-backed humanitarian aid. This USAID report was ignored by secretary of state Anthony Blinken in his address to Congress for more aid to Israel.

In this state of affairs, labor unions in the US face a historic responsibility. As SUNY BDS Labor Alliance, we reject the concept that labor unions are merely organizations of a narrow economic focus, whose only task is to bargain every few years and bureaucratically enforce contracts. Labor unions are organizations of the working class, and working class solidarity should not be limited either by workplace nor national borders. Labor unions historically have been and continue to be key institutions for workers to act collectively against exploitative and oppressive conditions, whether against wars, apartheid systems, or systemic racism and discrimination. The labor movement has a long history of solidarity with the struggle for liberation globally. From apartheid South Africa to the US civil rights movement, union members have marched, joined boycotts, lobbied politicians, and raised our collective voices to dismantle oppressive systems. We have refused our labor when it would further an amoral goal.

We thereby believe that standing against war, genocide, apartheid, and oppression are not exogenous matters for labor unions, these are integral aspects of the responsibilities and interests of workers who are now more internationally connected than ever. This is especially important for labor unions in countries like the US, whose corporations exploit cheap labor and resources all across the world, and facilitate war and genocide overseas. In this context, restricting our actions to incremental economic demands betrays international working-class solidarity and ignores the ways our collective structural power can challenge such affairs.

In line with these principles, scores of US labor unions are standing against Israel’s genocide, affirming Palestinian self-determination and calling for a ceasefire. On July 23, 2024, seven major US unions; Association of Flight Attendants (AFA), American Postal Workers Union (APWU), International Union of Painters (IUPAT), National Education Association (NEA), Service Employees International Union (SEIU), United Auto Workers (UAW), and United Electrical Workers (UE); which represent millions of workers, urged President Biden to end military aid to Israel.

Our labor unions reflect the diversity, in all senses, of the US public, whom the majority support an arms embargo against Israel.

It is past time that SUNY labor unions adopt a clear stance against genocide, ethnic cleansing, and apartheid in Palestine. Since the beginning of Israel’s genocide, SUNY system union members have been active participants of the SUNY BDS movement, and certain chapters and coalitions within our unions have been a driving force in organizing for Palestinian liberation. In terms of statewide commitment against genocide, though, SUNY unions have fallen behind many other examples. While individual chapters at Albany, Buffalo Center, Old Westbury, and Stony Brook issued unequivocal statements in support of the Palestinian people and their liberation, the statement endorsed by the UUP statewide Delegate Assembly made false moral equivalencies between the deliberate genocidal acts of the Israeli state and the acts of resistance against that genocide by the Palestinian people.

In 2023, GSEU issued in its chapters a poll that sought member approval for a ceasefire statement and for GSEU to partner with organizations on campuses that support Palestine. After overwhelming approval from membership in both instances, GSEU published a ceasefire statement that November. In May 2024, the Education Division of CWA 1104, to which RAU and GSEU belong, distributed a poll that asked its members to vote on whether the union “should join others in calling for SUNY, Fordham University, and the Research Foundation to divest from Israel.” At the end of the 3-day voting period, which lasted from May 7 to May 10, the union notified its membership that 87% of the participants voted in favor of divestment. However, it stated that “only about 4.6% of the bargaining unit members voted despite a long polling period. This makes it difficult for the Education Division to conclusively move forward as the result does not bear a representative sample.” A 3-day voting period is hardly a long polling period. We believe that the union should determine in advance a longer polling period, what percentage would indicate a representative sample, and varied methods for disseminating polls more widely. The union, though, noted that the results “indicate that there is a vocal interest in supporting such calls in the future, but to support those calls we will need more members to speak up and express interest.” This petition is just such a call.

We believe that these initiatives above in all our unions are simply not enough. As workers from various unions within the SUNY system, we are united in the SUNY BDS Labor Alliance, organizing to advance anti-imperialist, anti-war unionism and develop institutional support for Palestinian liberation within SUNY unions. The SUNY BDS call has already received the support of thousands of students, faculty and staff, alumni, community members and beyond, representing one of the most coordinated statewide movements in our education system for decades. On many SUNY campuses, both undergraduate and graduate student governments have advanced BDS resolutions, among them University at Albany, College of Environmental Science and Forestry (ESF), Binghamton University, Stony Brook University, Fashion Institution of Technology (FIT), and University at Buffalo.

It is past time that SUNY labor takes a collective stand against genocide as labor and with its primary institutions, our labor unions.

Thereby, as SUNY education workers, we demand:

UUP, RAU, and GSEU join the growing call from unions across the world to stop the genocide against Palestinians, and make a clear stance against the ongoing ethnic cleansing of Palestinians from their land.

UUP, RAU, and GSEU call for an end to the siege on Gaza and demand ongoing provision of humanitarian aid to Palestinians.

UUP, RAU, and GSEU call on the US government to act according to its own laws, particularly the Leahy law, to stop military aid to Israel.

UUP, RAU, and GSEU publicly declare support for the BDS (Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions) movement. We join the call for SUNY to adopt BDS measures.

UUP, RAU, and GSEU make earnest, clear effort for a visible display of the preceding institutional positions. This can be accomplished by placing their relative statements and value commitments in their website, sharing them with members, making social media posts, communicating this commitment as part of the union’s fundamental values when introducing the unions to new workers in orientations, prominently featuring them in its newsletters etc.

UUP, RAU, and GSEU internally ensure that our funding, dues, and investments follow BDS measures.

UUP, RAU, and GSEU strongly commit to supporting members who face retaliation in response to their support for Palestinian liberation.

UUP, RAU, and GSEU use our organizational capacities and resources to advance messaging and education initiatives against genocide and war, and which supports international solidarity and Palestinian liberation. This can include partnering officially with other campus organizations, hosting events, distributing messaging, devoting resources and organizing special committees within the unions in accordance with these purposes.

*SUNY BDS is proudly not affiliated with SUNY or NYS.

title: Pressure Campaigns: How Boycotts and Direct Action Are Challenging Corporate Power [Labor for Palestine-LA.OC.IE, Entertainment Labor for Palestine] (LAProgressive)
content:
At the 2026 Left Coast Forum, organizers behind the Home Depot, Hilton, Spotify, Citizens Bank, and Hollywood boycott campaigns shared how economic pressure, coalition building, and strategic disruption can force powerful institutions to respond.

What happens when activists stop asking corporations to do the right thing and start making it expensive for them to do the wrong thing?

That question was at the heart of “Pressure Campaigns: The Power of Boycotts and Direct Action,” a panel at the fourth annual Left Coast Forum, held October 2–4, 2026, at Cal State Los Angeles.

Moderated by MaryLinda Moss, artist, activist, and founding member of NELA Alliance for Democracy, the discussion brought together Miriam Arghandiwal, an organizer with the Boycott Home Depot Coalition and Entertainment Labor for Palestine; Chris Abrahamsen, co-founder of Grassroots Activist International Association and regional director of ICEBreakers; and Robby Kumar, a former investment banker and congressional staffer working with De-ICE Citizens Bank and No Camps California.

Their campaigns target different industries, but share a central premise: Corporations respond to financial incentives, public scrutiny, and the possibility of losing customers, investors, and business relationships.

The panelists described how ordinary people can use those vulnerabilities to challenge institutions with vastly greater financial and political resources.

Arghandiwal described the Boycott Home Depot Coalition’s campaign against the retailer over immigration enforcement raids targeting day laborers in its parking lots.

The boycott, initiated by Unión del Barrio, calls on Home Depot to publicly condemn ICE operations, prevent immigration enforcement activities on its properties where legally possible, provide safe hiring areas for day laborers, compensate affected families, and remove surveillance equipment and devices intended to discourage people from gathering.

Arghandiwal said organizers have documented more than 700 people taken into custody in connection with Home Depot locations across Southern California.

But she emphasized that pressure campaigns must protect the very people they are intended to support.

Demonstrations at stores where day laborers gather can inadvertently attract additional law enforcement, putting vulnerable workers at greater risk.

The coalition therefore developed guidelines requiring organizers to consult day laborers before staging protests and, when appropriate, conduct demonstrations at locations or times that minimize those risks.

The campaign has also pursued divestment. Arghandiwal reported that organizers helped secure the withdrawal of $20 million in Illinois investment funds from Home Depot and a smaller divestment commitment in West Hollywood.

These actions illustrate how consumer boycotts can extend into public investment decisions, increasing pressure beyond individual purchasing choices.

Arghandiwal also discussed Entertainment Labor for Palestine, which organizes in support of the Palestinian-led Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement.

Unlike conventional consumer campaigns, Hollywood pressure campaigns often focus on cultural influence, public reputation, and accountability within the entertainment industry.

Organizers have demonstrated at the Academy Awards, protested film premieres, and challenged entertainment companies over their treatment of artists who publicly support Palestinian rights.

Arghandiwal cited protests surrounding Scream 7, following the firing of actress Melissa Barrera over social media statements concerning Gaza.

She described efforts to sustain public attention throughout the film’s promotional campaign, including demonstrations at its premiere.

Entertainment Labor for Palestine also participated in protests surrounding Disney productions, including Captain America: Brave New World and Snow White.

For Arghandiwal, success is not measured exclusively in immediate box-office losses.

Changing what studios, executives, and performers consider reputationally acceptable can influence future decisions even when the financial consequences are difficult to calculate.

Her broader argument was that sustained public resistance can make controversial corporate decisions harder to normalize.

Chris Abrahamsen offered one of the panel’s clearest examples of a campaign with a specific corporate demand and a reported measurable outcome.

When Spotify began running ICE recruitment advertisements, organizers quickly mobilized demonstrations demanding that the streaming platform stop carrying them.

Abrahamsen described a campaign involving weekly protests outside Spotify offices, extensive outreach to musicians, and highly visible demonstrations using washable simulated blood to symbolize the suffering organizers associated with immigration enforcement.

The coalition also encouraged consumers to switch to competing streaming services.

An important part of the strategy involved what Abrahamsen called tertiary targets: influential people or organizations capable of pressuring the corporation even when its executives refused to engage directly.

In Spotify’s case, those targets included musicians whose participation was essential to the platform’s business.

After approximately 11 weeks, Spotify stopped running the advertisements.

Abrahamsen attributed the outcome to sustained organizing, although he acknowledged that Spotify did not publicly credit the protests for its decision.

He estimated that the advertising contract was worth approximately $78,000, compared with roughly $2,000 in campaign materials.

For the organizers, the episode demonstrated the potential leverage of a relatively small, coordinated campaign.https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/6SKYpS7z9s4?enablejsapi=1

Following the Spotify campaign, Abrahamsen’s organizing network turned its attention to Hilton hotels over accommodations provided to immigration enforcement personnel.

The campaign demands that Hilton refuse room bookings paid for with government purchasing cards associated with ICE or the Department of Homeland Security and disclose the financial extent of those arrangements.

Organizers have staged repeated demonstrations at Hilton properties, including actions inside hotel lobbies.

Unlike Spotify, where customers could easily switch streaming platforms, Hilton presents a more complicated target involving individual properties, hotel management, and government purchasing arrangements.

Abrahamsen argued that demonstrations generate costs beyond the immediate disruption: additional security, staffing, management attention, and the potential loss of customers.

He stressed the importance of choosing campaigns with achievable demands and maintaining pressure until those demands are addressed.

The strategic calculation, as he described it, is whether organizers can make continued corporate participation in a disputed activity more expensive than withdrawing from it.

Robby Kumar brought a different perspective to the discussion.

Drawing on his background in investment banking, he explained why targeting individual customers is only one way to pressure financial institutions.

De-ICE Citizens Bank has challenged Citizens Bank over its financial relationships with private prison corporations GEO Group and CoreCivic.

While activists initially concentrated on convincing individual customers to withdraw deposits and close accounts, Kumar encouraged a focus on municipal governments and other institutional banking customers.

The potential financial impact was substantially greater.

According to Kumar, Jersey City approved withdrawing approximately $265 million from Citizens Bank, while Montclair, New Jersey, moved to withdraw another $91 million.

He also cautioned against prematurely declaring victory.

When Citizens Bank announced that it would discontinue certain lending facilities involving the private prison companies, some organizers considered the campaign successful.

Kumar disagreed with treating that announcement as a complete break.

He argued that changes in the companies’ financing needs, following federal purchases of detention facilities, complicated the significance of the bank’s decision. Citizens Bank had not necessarily ended every financial relationship with the companies.

His lesson was important: A campaign must define success precisely enough to distinguish a substantive corporate change from a public-relations announcement.

Throughout the discussion, speakers returned to the importance of organizing across movements.

The campaigns against immigration enforcement, corporate financing, and Israel’s treatment of Palestinians frequently intersect through shared institutions, contractors, and financial relationships.

But coalition building requires judgment.

Arghandiwal emphasized that confrontational demonstrations may be inappropriate when they expose day laborers or undocumented communities to additional danger.

Abrahamsen similarly explained that disruptive action groups sometimes need to operate separately from organizations providing direct services to vulnerable immigrants.

Cooperation does not require identical tactics.

Instead, effective coalitions can share research, coordinate messaging, identify financial pressure points, and support one another while respecting the different risks facing their members.

The panel concluded with practical lessons about strategy.

Successful pressure campaigns, the speakers suggested, begin by identifying who makes the decisions, what those decision-makers value, which relationships give others leverage over them, and what specific concessions would constitute a victory.

They also require persistence, creativity, public visibility, and a willingness to adapt.

The discussion demonstrated that economic resistance is not limited to refusing purchases. It can involve persuading municipalities to move millions in public deposits, pressuring artists to challenge streaming platforms, demanding accountability from entertainment companies, or organizing customers around corporate contracts.

The larger lesson of the Left Coast Forum panel was that power does not reside exclusively in corporate boardrooms or government offices.

Consumers, workers, artists, investors, and communities also exercise economic power.

The challenge is to organize that power collectively, strategically, and long enough to make a difference.

That same day, solidarity events ranging from fundraising dinners to public meetings took place in 28 cities around the world, from New Haven, Connecticut, to Manchester, England.

This growing labor support reflects an understanding of what is at stake: the indictments of the MN15 are not simply an attack on 15 individuals. They are an attack on the ability of workers to organize collectively against government repression.

title: Dockworkers Do Not Work For War — 30 October International Day of Action (No Harbour For Genocide et al)
content:
A post shared by No Harbour For Genocide (@noharbour4genocide)

On 30 October, dockworkers in more than 45 ports internationally will be take action against war and genocide.

Eight unions from France, Greece, Cyprus, the Basque Country, Türkiye, Morocco and Italy will refuse to let their ports be used to send weapons to war. They’re inviting port unions everywhere to join them.

They’re also taking action over their own working conditions. Dockworkers are being pushed into longer hours and seven-day weeks, secure jobs are being replaced with subcontracted and insecure work, and automation and AI are being used to cut jobs, all while pay falls further behind the cost of fuel, energy and food.

They’re asking for three things: no weapons or troops sent to war through their ports, no turning ports into military bases, and money spent on wages, safe jobs and pensions instead of weapons.

Save the date and share this post. Stay tuned, we’ll be sharing more on how ports work and how you can support the workers.

title: Over 200 organisations across more than 60 countries unite in Global Mobilisation for Palestine on 10 October (Middle East Monitor)
content:
LONDON — More than 200 civil society organisations, trade unions, student federations, human rights networks and grassroots groups across six continents will mobilise for Palestine on Saturday, 10 October, in a coordinated day of action spanning more than 60 countries.

Convened by the Global Alliance for Palestine, with the support of the Anti-Apartheid Movement (AAM) and the Global Coalition against Occupation of Palestine (SANED), this coordinated action seeks to create a unified, direct civil intervention intended to interrupt public complicity and demand systemic accountability against Israel’s war crimes and crimes against humanity. The Global Day of Action brings together markedly different forms of mobilisation under a shared international framework.

The scale of the mobilisation is reflected not only in the number of countries taking part, but in the variety of actions being organised. From major demonstrations in cities including London, Sydney/Warrane, Cape Town, São Paulo, Rabat, Quito, Mexico City, Istanbul, Santiago, Reykjavík and Bangkok, to blockades and interventions targeting government and commercial sites, multi-day cultural programmes, teach-ins, film screenings, vigils and student-led educational actions, the mobilisation will take markedly different forms across the countries taking part.
